title: Lesson planning is not a homogenous activity
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton opens with an early-career teacher spending three to four hours nightly building PowerPoints yet feeling her lessons still fall flat, and uses her to argue that lesson planning bundles four different activities: creation, curation, adaptation and preparation. Through four department case studies he shows the costs of each emphasis and endorses the model described by Greg Ashman, in which a team collaboratively builds central lessons and teachers are obliged to spend their saved time on preparation. The argument is aimed at department leaders responsible for teacher workload and consistency. The piece is useful for anyone deciding how much planning should be done individually and how much shared across a department.
points: Splitting planning into creation, curation, adaptation and preparation shows why hours of effort can still leave teachers unready for the lesson itself.
Curating good resources is a complex skill that novices lack, and the sum of curated parts is not always a coherent lesson.
A shared central PowerPoint breeds complacency unless teachers must work through the questions and rehearse explanations.
Ratcheting improvement comes from collaboratively built lessons plus shared assessment outliers that prompt colleagues to demonstrate what worked.
quotes: She said she spent three to four hours each night planning lessons for the following day and then felt disheartened when her lessons did not go as well as she liked.
She had no answers to these questions because she had not thought about them. Instead, she had spent over 2 hours creating a lesson, but much less time, if any, preparing for that lesson.

Lesson planning is not a homogenous activity. Having worked with many teachers over the last twenty years and reflecting on my evolving lesson-planning process, I think four distinct activities get lumped under the term lesson planning.
In this day and age, with high–quality lesson materials available at low or zero cost, this simply should not be happening. The department leadership team is responsible for ensuring it doesn’t.

But there is a catch. I don’t think we fully appreciate what a complex skill high-quality lesson curation is. First, there is the challenge of identifying what a good resource is. Do we go off who created it? Or how pretty it looks? Second, there is the challenge of assembling high-quality resources from several different sources into a coherent flow and sequence that will lead to a high-quality learning experience for our students.

The worst case of this I ever saw was a head of department clicking through a White Rose Maths PowerPoint and being visibly shocked when he saw a question appear on the screen that neither he nor his students had any idea how to answer.

I have never planned a lesson that did not improve having shown it to a colleague. Even talking through the choice of examples or the logic of the question sequencing leads to realisations and subsequent changes that would have stayed invisible without such prompting. Whether lessons are created by individuals and then shared for comments, or created by teams, I firmly believe this leads to higher quality materials than can be achieved by even the strongest teacher working alone.
